title: Identify the need for capital and understand the need for the recording of the income and different costs in an agri-business

lessons.title: Capital: the money and things you need to farm
lessons.html:
What capital is

Capital is the money and the things of value that a farmer needs to start and run a farm business. Without capital, you cannot buy seed, feed or tools, and you cannot farm.

Kinds of capital

KindExamplesHow long it lasts
Land and buildingsFields, chicken house, store room, kraalMany years
EquipmentWheelbarrow, spade, knapsack sprayer, water tank, pump, bakkieSeveral years
Breeding animalsCows, ewes, sows, goatsSeveral years
Working moneyMoney for seed, fertiliser, feed, medicine, fuel, wagesUsed up in one season

Why a farmer needs capital

  • To start – fence, water, a chicken house, tools.
  • To run the farm – buy inputs before there is anything to sell. A farmer plants cabbages and pays for seedlings and fertiliser now, but only gets paid when the cabbages are sold months later.
  • To grow – buy more animals, more land or better equipment.
  • To survive bad times – drought or disease can stop income for a while.

Where capital comes from

  • Your own savings.
  • Profit from the farm, kept in the business.
  • Family or partners.
  • Loans from a bank, a co-op or a development agency. A loan must be paid back with interest.
  • Government grants and support programmes.
  • Stokvels and savings groups.

Before you borrow, make sure the enterprise will make enough money to pay back the loan and interest on time.

Example

Thabo wants to start 100 layer hens. He needs capital for a hen house, feeders and drinkers (lasting many years), the hens themselves, and working money for feed until the hens start laying and the eggs are sold.

lessons.title: Recording income and costs
lessons.html:
Why keep records?

Many small farmers do not know if they are making a profit or a loss, because they do not write down what they spend and what they earn. Records help you:

  • Know if the enterprise makes a profit.
  • See which costs are biggest, so you can try to cut them.
  • Plan for next season.
  • Show a bank or support programme how your farm is doing.
  • Keep business money and household money apart.

Income

Income is money coming in: selling vegetables, eggs, animals, milk or services such as ploughing for a neighbour.

Different kinds of costs

  • Variable costs go up and down with how much you produce: seed, seedlings, fertiliser, feed, medicine, packaging, transport to market. More chickens means more feed.
  • Fixed costs stay the same whether you produce a lot or a little: rent, loan repayments, insurance, a permanent worker's wage.
  • Capital costs are for things that last many years, such as a water tank or a pump.

A simple record book

DateDetailsMoney in (R)Money out (R)
3 MayBought 500 cabbage seedlings450
3 MayBought fertiliser600
20 JuneTransport to market250
21 JuneSold 200 cabbages2,400
28 JuneSold 250 cabbages3,000
Totals5,4001,300

Money in minus money out: R5,400 minus R1,300 = R4,100. This is before paying for your own time, water and other costs, so write those down too.

Good habits

  • Write each sale and payment on the same day.
  • Keep all slips and receipts in an envelope or file.
  • Add up totals every month.
  • Do not take farm money for household use without writing it down.

Key points

  • Capital is the money and things of value needed to farm.
  • Capital is needed to start, run, grow and survive bad times.
  • Borrow only if the farm can pay back the loan and interest.
  • Costs can be variable, fixed or capital.
  • Record every sale and payment to know your profit.
